description: We founded the PhysiCAL team in 2021 and won the CERN Beamline for Schools competition in 2025, then conducted our experiment at CERN T10 Beamline. We also presented our experiment results at RADECS 2026 with our poster.
summary:
Cities rarely announce that they are sinking. It shows through a cracked wall, a door that no longer closes, a monument that needs another step. SinkWatch turns those quiet signs into a measurement anyone can read. We stack NISAR’s 12-day L-band radar interferograms into one continuous record of centimeter-scale ground motion, combining ascending and descending orbits to separate true vertical sinking from sideways drift.

We tested it in Mexico City. Eleven months of NISAR data (November 2025 to October 2026) show Xochimilco–Tláhuac and Chalco dropping more than 35 cm a year while bedrock control points stay still. The cause is not nature. It is us: around 63% of the water used by 23 million people is pumped from the aquifer beneath their feet.

Mexico City is only the first step. Wherever irrigation wells run without limits, or industry draws more than the ground can give back, the land keeps the record. Overpumping is invisible at the well, but from orbit it leaves a fingerprint that cannot be hidden. SinkWatch reads it, so communities, journalists and regulators can ask who is taking the water. One city today; every city NISAR passes over tomorrow.
details:
What it does and how it works. Cities rarely announce that they are sinking. SinkWatch makes it visible: it turns NISAR radar data into an interactive map of sinking ground in Mexico City. We processed 54 real NISAR L-band L2 GUNW interferograms, mostly 12 days apart. Combining an ascending track (19) and a descending track (113) separates true vertical sinking from sideways drift, giving one continuous record of 28 dates over eleven months (Nov 2025 – Oct 2026). NISAR GCOV HH and HV images add context: they show where the surface is city, fields or water, and so where the measurement can be trusted. In the browser, users press play to watch the ground drop, click any place for its total sinking, yearly rate and chart, and compare our rates with published studies. A tilt view shows where neighbouring ground sinks at different speeds.

Benefits. Anyone can read it: no radar expertise and no software install, just a browser. It is honest about limits: where the signal breaks up, the map says “no measurement”, not “no sinking”. We checked the method against bedrock control points, which stay within one centimetre of zero a year, and compared our rates with published Sentinel-1 studies and NASA/JPL’s early NISAR map.

Intended impact. The sinking we measure is not a natural disaster. It is a human one: the ground falls because more water is pumped out of the aquifer than returns to it. Cracked walls and broken pipes appear where neighbours sink at different speeds, and the people who live there are rarely the ones who decided how much to pump. Mexico City is only our first step. The same thing happens wherever irrigation wells run without limits or industry draws more than the ground can give back. Overpumping is invisible at the well, but from orbit it leaves a fingerprint that cannot be hidden. NISAR delivers free, ready-processed data every 12 days, so the same approach can become routine early warning for civil engineers, water agencies, residents and reporters, in any city or groundwater basin the satellite passes over. Our goal is that anyone can ask where the ground is falling, how fast, and who is taking the water.

Tools. Python (NumPy, SciPy, h5py, Matplotlib, Pillow) to process NISAR GUNW and GCOV products from the Alaska Satellite Facility into web-ready layers; React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS and Leaflet for the interactive map; deployed on Vercel. Esri map tiles and published studies provide context.

Creativity. We show the physics, not only the picture: real interferogram fringes, a swipe comparison of two polarizations, and a tilt layer that highlights differential sinking, which is what actually damages buildings. The map and basemap views are built for readers, not specialists.

Factors we considered. Data is provisional, so we flag it as such. Our rates sit near, not on, published values because periods, sensors and locations differ. We pre-registered our tilt validation criteria and reported the result honestly. SinkWatch measures the ground, not the wells: it shows where and how fast, and leaves the question of responsibility to those who can investigate it.
dataRefs: NASA/JPL 2026, “US-Indian space mission maps extreme subsidence in Mexico City”
